name: Platforms & Architectures
description: Windows, macOS, Android, iOS and the ARM vs x86 divide — what differs where, and why it matters to your code.

modules.name: Desktop & Architecture
modules.description: Windows and macOS internals, and the instruction sets underneath.

cards.answer: ARM is a RISC design with fixed-width instructions and a weaker memory model; x86-64 is CISC with variable-length instructions and a strong (TSO) memory model.

left.title: ARM (AArch64)
points: Weak memory ordering — needs explicit barriers

right.title: x86-64
points: Total store order — most reorderings forbidden

cards.explanation: The memory model difference is the practical trap: racy code that 'works' on x86 can fail on ARM because stores are reordered. Data races were always bugs; ARM just makes them visible. Always test on the architecture you deploy to.

resources.title: Preshing — Weak vs strong memory models

cards.prompt: Practical differences between Windows and Unix-like systems for developers
cards.answer: Path separators and case sensitivity, line endings, process creation, file locking and permissions models all differ.

left.title: Windows
points: Files locked while open; ACLs, not mode bits

right.title: Unix-like
points: Open files can be deleted; user/group/other mode bits

cards.explanation: The bugs this causes: a rename that fails because a handle is open, a git checkout where `README` and `readme` collide, and CRLF diffs. Use path libraries rather than string concatenation, and set `core.autocrlf` deliberately.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Naming files, paths, and namespaces

cards.prompt: What is WSL2, and what is the main performance trap?
cards.answer: A real Linux kernel running in a lightweight VM with tight Windows integration. The trap is cross-filesystem I/O: working on `/mnt/c/...` from Linux (or on the Linux filesystem from Windows tools) goes through a 9p/plan9 bridge and is dramatically slower.
cards.explanation: Keep project files inside the Linux filesystem (`~/code`) when using Linux tooling. Node installs, git status and file watchers are the operations that feel this worst — often by an order of magnitude.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — WSL file system performance

cards.prompt: Your macOS app downloads fine but users see 'cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified'. What is missing?
cards.answer: Code signing with a Developer ID certificate and notarisation by Apple, with the ticket stapled to the artefact. Gatekeeper checks both on first launch.
cards.explanation: The quarantine attribute (`com.apple.quarantine`) is what triggers the check on downloaded files. The equivalent on Windows is Authenticode signing plus SmartScreen reputation; unsigned binaries are increasingly unusable on both platforms.

resources.title: Apple — Notarizing macOS software before distribution

modules.name: Mobile Platforms
modules.description: Android and iOS lifecycles, permissions and the constraints that shape mobile code.

cards.prompt: Why does the app lifecycle dominate mobile development?
cards.answer: The OS can suspend or kill your process at any time to reclaim resources, and it recreates UI on configuration changes. Anything not saved to persistent state can vanish between one screen and the next.
cards.explanation: Android recreates activities on rotation, locale change and theme change; iOS suspends in the background and terminates under memory pressure. Hold state in a lifecycle-aware holder (ViewModel, SceneStorage) and treat 'the process may die here' as normal.

cards.prompt: How should an app request a sensitive permission such as location?
cards.answer: Ask in context, at the moment the feature needs it, after explaining why — and handle every outcome: granted, denied, denied permanently, and 'while using the app' or approximate-only.
cards.explanation: Both platforms let users grant reduced access (coarse location, one-time, limited photo selection), so a binary granted/denied assumption is wrong. A permission prompt fired on first launch with no context is the reliable way to get denied forever.

cards.prompt: What drains mobile battery most, and what is the standard mitigation?
cards.answer: Radio wakeups (each network request keeps the cellular radio powered for seconds afterwards), GPS, wake locks and background work. Mitigate by batching and deferring network calls, coalescing sync with system schedulers, and using push instead of polling.
cards.explanation: WorkManager on Android and BGTaskScheduler on iOS let the OS batch your work with everyone else's wakeups. Both platforms will simply refuse or throttle background work that ignores this — 'it works in debug' is not evidence.

cards.prompt: Native, React Native, Flutter or a web app — how do you decide?
cards.answer: By how much the product depends on platform-specific capability and feel. Deep hardware/OS integration and demanding UI push native; a mostly-forms app on a small team pushes cross-platform; content that needs no install pushes web or PWA.
cards.explanation: Cross-platform frameworks share business logic well and diverge on the last 10% — platform conventions, new OS features on day one, and specialised hardware. Budget for native modules; teams that assume 100% sharing rebuild twice.

modules.name: Developer Environments Across Platforms
modules.description: Package managers, Linux distributions, Windows and macOS service models, shells, dotfiles and app sandboxing.

cards.prompt: Which package managers do you meet on each platform, and what should you avoid mixing?
cards.answer: Linux: apt/dpkg (Debian, Ubuntu), dnf/rpm (Fedora, RHEL), pacman (Arch), apk (Alpine). macOS: Homebrew. Windows: winget, Scoop, Chocolatey. Language ecosystems add their own (npm, pip, cargo) and version managers (nvm, pyenv, mise, asdf).
cards.explanation: Avoid installing language packages globally with the system package manager and the language tool at once — the two fight over the same files. Keep the OS for system software and per-project tools (virtualenvs, local node_modules, mise) for application dependencies.

cards.prompt: Debian/Ubuntu vs RHEL-family vs Alpine as a server or container base
cards.answer: Debian and Ubuntu (apt, glibc) have the broadest package ecosystem and documentation; RHEL and its rebuilds (Rocky, Alma — dnf, glibc) offer long enterprise support; Alpine (apk, musl libc) is tiny and popular for containers.
cards.explanation: musl differs from glibc in DNS resolution, locale handling and performance, and prebuilt binaries (Python wheels, Node native modules) may not exist for it — so Alpine images can build slower or behave differently. Debian slim or distroless images are a common safer default.

resources.title: Docker docs — Choosing a base image

cards.prompt: Running a background service: systemd (Linux) vs launchd (macOS) vs Windows Services
cards.answer: All three start processes at boot or login, restart them on failure and run them without a user session, but each has its own format: systemd unit files, launchd property-list files, and the Windows Service Control Manager (managed with `sc`, PowerShell or NSSM).
cards.explanation: Cross-platform tools either abstract these (Node's pm2, the kardianos Go service library) or run in containers so the host's init system matters less. Log destinations differ too: journald, unified logging (`log show`) and the Windows Event Log.

resources.title: Apple — Creating launch daemons and agents

cards.prompt: What is fundamentally different about PowerShell compared with Bash?
cards.answer: PowerShell pipes .NET *objects*, not text: `Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100 | Sort-Object CPU` filters and sorts on typed properties without parsing columns. Commands follow a Verb-Noun convention and share a consistent parameter model.
cards.explanation: Structured pipelines remove fragile `awk`/`cut` parsing, at the cost of different habits. PowerShell 7 is cross-platform. Escaping and quoting rules differ from Bash — the backtick is the escape character — which trips people moving between them.

cards.prompt: A new laptop takes you two days to set up and every machine behaves slightly differently. How do you fix that?
cards.answer: Keep dotfiles (shell, git, editor config) in a git repository and apply them with a tool (chezmoi, GNU Stow, or a bootstrap script), and pin project toolchains per repo (mise/asdf `.tool-versions`, `.nvmrc`, dev containers or Nix) so the project declares what it needs.
cards.explanation: Reproducible environments are the local equivalent of infrastructure as code. Dev containers go furthest — the whole toolchain in an image the editor attaches to — so "works on my machine" becomes "works in the declared environment".

cards.prompt: How do modern desktop and mobile platforms sandbox applications?
cards.answer: Apps run with limited default access and must declare or request capabilities: iOS and Android sandboxes with permission prompts; the macOS App Sandbox with entitlements plus TCC prompts for camera, files and screen recording; Windows AppContainer for Store apps; Flatpak and Snap on Linux.
cards.explanation: Sandboxing contains the damage of a compromised or malicious app. For developers it means requesting the narrowest entitlements, handling denial gracefully, and expecting file access to go through system pickers rather than arbitrary paths.
